title: 1 Introduction
content:
Organizational Behaviour, or OB, is the study of how people act within organizations and how their actions affect the organization’s overall performance. It’s about understanding what individuals do, how groups interact, and how the structure of an organization influences behaviour. This knowledge helps managers and leaders create better workplaces and improve productivity. At its core, OB looks at three main things: individuals, groups, and organizational structure, and how these interact to shape work and workplace culture.

When we talk about work, it’s important to realize it’s more than just a way to earn money. Work is any activity that produces something valuable for others. It serves several purposes: it provides income, connects us socially, gives us status in our community, and often becomes a big part of our identity. Work can boost our self-esteem because it lets us show what we’re capable of and feel that we’re contributing something meaningful. For some people, work is also a way to grow and reach their full potential. But when work doesn’t provide these things, people can feel alienated—they might feel powerless, disconnected, or like their efforts don’t matter.

Organizational Behaviour studies these human aspects in organizations. Simply put, it looks at what people do at work and how their behaviour affects the organization’s success. While human behaviour is complex and sometimes hard to predict, OB finds patterns that help us understand and sometimes anticipate how people will act. It covers topics like motivation, leadership, communication, group dynamics, attitudes, change, conflict, and how jobs are designed.

OB draws from several fields to get a full picture. Psychology helps us understand individual behaviour and mental processes. Sociology shows us how society and social groups influence people. Social psychology looks at how groups affect individuals. Anthropology studies cultural rituals and traditions that shape behaviour. Political science examines power and authority in organizations. More recently, neuroscience has added insights about how the brain influences decision-making. Among these, psychology is often the most important because it focuses directly on individual behaviour.

The formal study of OB began with scientific management, but a key moment was the Hawthorne Studies in the 1920s and 1930s. These experiments looked at how different working conditions affected productivity. Surprisingly, they found that productivity improved not just because of physical changes like lighting but because workers felt observed and valued. This showed that human relations and feeling important mattered a lot. The “Hawthorne effect” describes how people change their behaviour when they know they’re being watched, highlighting the social and psychological side of work.

One important thing to remember is that unlike physical sciences, OB doesn’t have absolute laws that apply everywhere. People are different, and behaviour depends on the situation. So, what works in one place might not work in another. OB concepts need to be applied with an understanding of the specific context.

A useful way to think about organizations is like an iceberg. The visible part—the formal rules, structures, and roles—is just the tip. Below the surface are the hidden parts: people’s attitudes, informal relationships, unwritten rules, and culture. These hidden aspects often have a bigger impact on how well an organization works than the visible parts. Understanding this helps managers realize that managing people is more complicated than managing processes.

Management itself is about bringing all these pieces together. Managers coordinate and guide people’s efforts toward the organization’s goals. This is tricky because people aren’t just resources; they bring their own feelings, attitudes, and perceptions. Good management means understanding both the people and the organization and finding ways to align them.

For managers, knowing OB means using research and evidence rather than guesswork to understand behaviour. It helps improve communication and leadership skills, use data to make decisions, and stay updated on new trends. It also means empowering employees, managing change well, and helping people balance work and life. Managers should be aware that culture affects behaviour, especially in international settings, and that behaviour is influenced by individual, group, and organizational factors. Paying attention to all these levels makes management more effective.

In short, Organizational Behaviour helps us understand the human side of work. It shows that work is about more than tasks—it’s about people’s identities, motivations, and social connections. By studying individuals, groups, and structures, OB gives managers tools to create better workplaces where people can be productive and satisfied.

title: 2 Attitudes
content:
In any organization, the individual is the most important part. Organizations are made up of people, each with their own unique backgrounds, personalities, and ways of thinking. Understanding this individuality is key because it affects how people behave and interact at work. These differences can be a source of creativity and satisfaction, but they can also lead to conflict if not managed well. That’s why managers need to be good at selecting and developing people who will fit well and add value. They also need to understand themselves, including how their own personality affects others. Managing relationships at work has always been important, but with rapid changes happening in organizations and the world, it’s even more critical now. When changes feel forced or come from outside, managing people requires extra care and sensitivity. People may develop new attitudes and ways of thinking to cope with these changes. Managers also need to recognize the stress employees feel during these times, while managing their own stress as well. People differ in many ways—such as their culture, gender, personality, motivation, and intelligence—and all these factors influence how they behave at work.

Attitudes are basically how a person views and feels about something, whether it’s a person, an idea, or a situation. For example, when someone says, “I like my job,” they are expressing their attitude toward work. Attitudes are important because they influence how people respond and behave. There are different ideas about how attitudes form. One idea is that attitudes are part of a person’s personality and tend to be stable over time. Some people are naturally more positive or negative about their jobs regardless of the situation. Another idea is that attitudes depend on the situation. If someone has a bad boss or boring work, they might develop a negative attitude because of those experiences. A third idea is that attitudes come from the social environment—how people perceive the social context around them shapes their attitudes. In reality, all these ideas have some truth. People’s attitudes come from a mix of their personality and the social environment they are in.

Beliefs and values are related but different. Beliefs are about what we think is true or real, like believing hard work leads to success. Values are about what we think should be important or desirable, like valuing honesty. Together, beliefs and values shape our attitudes and how we behave.

Attitudes have three parts: what we think (cognition), how we feel (affect), and how we intend to act (behavior). For example, if someone thinks their pay is low, feels angry about it, and plans to look for another job, those are the three parts of their attitude. These parts are connected and influence each other, but they can be hard to separate. Sometimes we don’t fully understand why we feel or act a certain way.

People usually want their actions to match their attitudes. When they don’t, it creates discomfort called cognitive dissonance. For example, if someone acts in a way that doesn’t fit their beliefs, they feel uneasy. To fix this, they try to justify their behavior or change their attitude to feel better.

At work, people have many attitudes about their jobs. The most studied ones are job satisfaction, job involvement, and organizational commitment. Job satisfaction is how positively or negatively someone feels about their job overall. It’s influenced by many factors, like the work itself, pay, chances for promotion, supervision, and coworkers. If a job meets or exceeds a person’s expectations, they tend to be satisfied. Managers often measure job satisfaction through surveys to understand how employees feel. Satisfied employees are more likely to stay and perform well, while dissatisfied ones might leave, complain, or reduce effort.

Job involvement is about how much a person cares about and identifies with their work. Psychological empowerment is related—it’s about how much employees feel they can influence their work, feel competent, find their job meaningful, and have autonomy.

Organizational commitment means a strong emotional attachment to the organization. It involves believing in the organization’s goals, being willing to work hard for it, and wanting to stay. This goes beyond just loyalty; it’s about truly caring about the organization.

Perceived organizational support is how much employees feel the organization values and supports them. When employees feel supported, they tend to show better behaviors, like helping others and being on time.

Employee engagement is the passion and enthusiasm people have for their work. Engaged employees put energy and attention into their jobs, while disengaged ones may just go through the motions. Unfortunately, only a minority of employees tend to be highly engaged.

Organizational citizenship behavior refers to voluntary actions employees take that go beyond their job duties, like helping coworkers or suggesting improvements. These behaviors improve morale and reduce the need for supervision. Managers who understand this can encourage positive contributions while avoiding burnout.

While these job attitudes are distinct, they often overlap because of personality and how they influence each other. Understanding these attitudes helps managers create better work environments and support employees more effectively.

title: 3 Personality
content:
Personality is basically the set of stable traits and characteristics that explain why people behave the way they do. These traits, like being independent, organized, or agreeable, help us understand why someone might act differently from another person in similar situations. Personality isn’t just random; it’s consistent over time and across different contexts, which is why it’s useful to study, especially in workplaces where understanding behavior can improve teamwork and management.

Personality develops from a mix of inherited factors and life experiences. On the hereditary side, things like your physical build, temperament, and energy levels are influenced by your genes. These biological factors set a foundation for your personality. However, personality isn’t fixed at birth. It changes, especially during adolescence, and tends to become more stable as people grow older. When a trait shows up repeatedly in many situations over time, we call it a personality trait, and it becomes a key part of how we describe someone.

To make sense of personality, psychologists have developed frameworks to categorize and measure traits. One popular tool is the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator, or MBTI. It sorts people into 16 personality types based on four pairs of traits: whether someone is outgoing or reserved, practical or imaginative, logical or emotional, and structured or spontaneous. While MBTI is widely used, it has its critics because it treats personality as fixed and doesn’t account for how people grow or change.

A more scientifically supported model is the Big Five, which breaks personality down into five broad traits: extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, emotional stability, and openness to experience. Extraversion measures how comfortable someone is with social interaction, agreeableness looks at how cooperative and kind a person is, conscientiousness reflects reliability and organization, emotional stability shows how well someone handles stress, and openness captures curiosity and creativity. These traits have been shown to predict behavior in work settings quite well.

Besides these, there are other personality traits that are less positive but important to understand, especially in organizations. These are often called the Dark Triad: Machiavellianism, narcissism, and psychopathy. Machiavellianism involves being manipulative and pragmatic, often using others to get ahead. Narcissism is about having an inflated sense of self-importance and needing constant admiration. Psychopathy is marked by a lack of empathy and guilt, with individuals often being charming but manipulative and willing to bully others to gain power. These traits can cause problems in workplaces but also explain some of the more difficult behaviors managers encounter.

It’s important to remember that personality doesn’t act alone; the situation matters a lot. The strength of a situation—how clear and strict the rules and expectations are—can either limit or allow personality traits to show through. In strong situations, like a formal meeting with strict rules, personality has less influence on behavior. In weaker situations, like hanging out with friends, personality plays a bigger role. Another idea is that certain situations “activate” specific traits. For example, a sales job with commission pay might bring out extraversion more than a routine office job.

Values are another key part of understanding behavior. They are the beliefs about what is important or desirable in life and guide how we judge right and wrong. Values come in two types: terminal values, which are the goals we want to achieve, like success or happiness, and instrumental values, which are the ways we behave to reach those goals, like being disciplined or honest. Our values influence how we act at work and how we make decisions, sometimes helping us and sometimes biasing us.

In the workplace, it’s not just about skills but also about how well a person’s personality and values fit with the job and the organization. The idea of person-job fit suggests that people are happier and stay longer when their personality matches the demands of their job. For example, someone who likes practical, hands-on work will be more satisfied in a technical role than in a social one. Similarly, person-organization fit means that employees whose values align with the company culture tend to be more satisfied and less likely to leave. This is why many companies now focus on hiring people who fit their culture, not just those with the right skills.

Finally, values are shaped by culture and environment, unlike personality, which is mostly inherited. Different countries and societies develop their own value systems, which affect how people behave at work. One well-known way to understand these differences is Hofstede’s cultural dimensions, which look at how national cultures vary in values related to work and management. This helps explain why people from different countries might approach teamwork, authority, and decision-making differently.

In short, personality and values are central to understanding human behavior, especially in organizations. Personality gives us a stable pattern of traits, values guide our judgments and decisions, and both interact with the environment and culture around us. Knowing this helps managers and employees work better together and create healthier workplaces.

title: 4 Emotions and Moods
content:
Emotions and moods are a big part of how we experience the world and interact with others, especially in the workplace. To start, emotions are intense feelings that happen quickly in response to something specific, like a comment from a coworker or a sudden event. Biologically, emotions involve chemicals released in our bodies that create a feedback loop between the brain and body, lasting only a few seconds. Feelings come after emotions—they’re what we experience as we start to think about and process those emotions. Feelings tend to last longer because they involve more reflection and a mix of emotions. Moods are different; they’re less intense than emotions and don’t always have a clear cause. They can last for hours or days and are influenced by things like the environment, our physical health, and what we’re focusing on mentally. The word “affect” is a broad term that covers all these feelings, including both emotions and moods.

When we talk about moods, it’s useful to think of them in two main categories: positive affect and negative affect. Positive affect includes feelings like excitement and enthusiasm, while negative affect includes feelings like stress and anxiety. People can experience these moods at different levels—someone might feel very energetic and happy (high positive affect) or bored and tired (low positive affect). Similarly, someone might feel very anxious (high negative affect) or calm and content (low negative affect). These mood states influence how we behave and perform, especially at work.

Emotions and moods aren’t just random; they play important roles in how we think and act. Many people assume emotions get in the way of rational thinking, but research shows emotions actually help us make sense of the world. For example, people who are in a negative mood might be better at spotting truthful information than those who are happy. Emotions also guide our sense of right and wrong. Feelings like guilt, sympathy, or anger often shape our moral judgments more than pure logic does.

What influences our emotions and moods? There are two main sources: who we are and what’s happening around us. Personality plays a big role—some people naturally feel emotions more deeply than others. Age matters too; older people tend to experience fewer negative emotions and have longer-lasting positive moods. Gender differences exist as well, with women generally showing emotions more openly and intensely than men, except for anger. On the other hand, our current situation also affects our mood. The time of day, for example, influences how positive or negative we feel, with positive moods usually peaking in the evening. The day of the week matters too—people tend to feel better on weekends and worse on Mondays. Surprisingly, weather doesn’t have much effect on most people’s moods. Stressful events, social activities, sleep quality, exercise, and even blood sugar levels all play a part in shaping how we feel at any given moment.

In the workplace, emotional labour is an important concept. It refers to the effort employees put into managing their emotions to meet job expectations. Sometimes, workers have to display emotions they don’t actually feel, like smiling when they’re upset. This is called surface acting. Deep acting is when they try to change their real feelings to match what they need to show. When there’s a big gap between what they feel and what they display, it creates emotional dissonance, which can be tiring and stressful.

Affective Events Theory helps explain how specific things that happen at work trigger emotional reactions, which then affect job performance and satisfaction. For example, getting praised might boost motivation, while a negative comment might lower commitment. People who are less emotionally stable tend to react more strongly to negative events, and the mood they’re already in can change how they respond.

Emotional intelligence, or EQ, is the ability to recognize, understand, and manage your own emotions and those of others. It’s different from IQ, which measures cognitive skills. EQ is about emotional skills that help with teamwork, communication, leadership, and handling conflicts. People with high emotional intelligence tend to create better work environments and perform better. Improving EQ involves personal strategies like mindfulness, journaling, deep breathing, exercise, and seeking social support. Organizations can help by offering training, coaching, feedback, promoting open communication, and encouraging teamwork. Leaders who model emotional intelligence set a positive example for others.

In short, emotions and moods are central to how we function both personally and professionally. Understanding them, managing emotional labour, and developing emotional intelligence can improve how we relate to others and how well we perform in our jobs.
